newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - Taiwan night-owl money trade thrives on margin.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Taiwan night-owl money trade thrives on margin.

text.p: When night falls and Taipei traffic slows to a snail's pace, some Taiwan currency dealers are just getting started -- firing off quotes and buy/sell orders from otherwise deserted trading rooms.
Round-the-clock margin trading is getting a boost this year as banks step up competition to tap growing customer interest in cross-currency business, banking sources say.
"Margin trading comes to life in the late afternoon hours when the London market opens," said one currency dealer. "The activity continues through the evening."
Taipei is eight hours ahead of London.
Margin trading of currencies, though legalised in Taiwan in 1991, has begun to take off only recently.

Morris Li, vice-president and emerging markets treasurer of U.S. giant Citibank's Taiwan office, said the island's relatively lacklustre currency trading has prompted restless dealing managers to seek new business.

A stable U.S. dollar in the first half of 1996 cut profits from proprietary trading and a flat Taiwan dollar since the turbulence from China's military exercises peaked in March have further depressed business volumes, Li said.
At the same time, dwindling derivatives business has starved banks of revenue. Li said onerous new reporting requirements for firms using derivatives were hurting the young market.

Courted by solicitous banks, currency speculators are happy to switch from poorly-regulated "bucket shops" to trade through banks. Some dealers estimate the market is growing as much as 20 percent a month.
RULES OF THE GAME

Margin transactions are all U.S. dollar-based against major trading currencies such as the mark, yen, Swiss franc, Australian dollar and Canadian dollar. Daily trading volume has averaged about $100 million in recent months, according to a source at Taiwan's central bank.
Margin trading in the Taiwan dollar is prohibited and securities brokerages are not allowed to trade currencies.
Banks vary in initial margin requirements and leverage.
Citibank, for example, sets an initial margin at US$100,000 which allows customers to trade up to $1 million.

Standard Chartered Bank's Taiwan margin-trade operation has a lower threshold and two classes of leverage. With a US$25,000 good-faith deposit, regular customers can trade 10 times the limit. For selected customers with "market savvy", a 20-times leverage is possible, said a dealer at the bank.
COMPETITION AND CAUTION
Under competitive pressure, some banks have gone out of their way to be flexible.
"Some foreign banks would not allow that extent of leverage in other markets, but they would do it in Taiwan for fear of losing to the competition," said a foreign bank dealer.
Foreign banks control the lion's share of margin accounts with domestic banks struggling to catch up, said Daniel Chen, chief economist at Chinatrust Commercial Bank.
"Foreign banks have an edge on us," Chen said. "They have always been more trading-oriented in the forex business."
The more conservative Taiwan banks are wary of the high leverage of margin trading, especially after highly-publicised derivatives losses, Chen said.

The unlisted Overseas Chinese Bank reported US$60 million in unrealised losses from derivatives trade in January 1995. First Bank, one of Taiwan's "big three" state-owned commercial banks, took a charge of US$20 million in June 1995 from derivatives trading over a four-year period.
"The truth is we don't have manpower to venture away from basic trade financing," said a domestic bank dealer, adding that Japanese banks also opt to stick to basic trade financing.
COMMODITIES BUSINESS
Li of Citibank took issue with critics who say margin trade puts banks at greater risk than other banking activities.
"Responsible banks do not approve anyone who has $50,000 or $100,000 to gamble away in margin trading," he said.
Margin trading is appropriate only for the investors who have a large capital cushion and a commitment to allocate a small portion of their assets to this high-risk high-return activity, Li noted.
Banks demand extra margin deposits in volatile markets and will close positions if these fail, he said.
Moreover, margin trading desks make back-to-back offsetting trades once a customer's order is executed.
"It's important that we lay off the risks quickly," Li said. "Access to the London market is important."
The Standard Chartered dealer agreed that margin trading is basically a commodities business: "We try to square off immediately and only make money on the bid/ask spreads."
SOBERING THOUGHTS
Some dealers see margin trading's explosive growth slowing.
"New customers, especially smaller accounts, will learn after a while that many trades are awash," said a foreign bank dealer. "You don't need a disaster to wake them up."

In currency trades, a transaction fee is implied in the bid/ask spread. Broken-size -- less than $1 million -- trades carry larger spreads. And retail customers are prone to buying high and selling low in a volatile market, he said.
To advise and manage the new crop of margin investors, small time bucket shop operators and ex-dealers have become currency investment consultants, though few have proven records.
"It's going to be a while before you get the size of even a minor league hedge fund," a foreign bank dealer said.
